hints: Notice the incoming nucleus moves exactly horizontally while the target is stationary, so total momentum perpendicular to that line is initially zero.
Think about vector addition of the two final momenta and what their up-or-down components must add to for an isolated collision in vacuum.
Compare the four diagrams for whether the two outgoing tracks are on opposite sides of the incoming line or both on the same side.
walkthrough: Identify the system: one nucleus moving horizontally and one stationary, with no external forces in vacuum, so total vector momentum $p$ is conserved in the collision.
Resolve momentum perpendicular to the incoming direction. Initially this component is zero because motion is purely along the horizontal line.
After collision the vector sum of the perpendicular components must therefore also be zero: $p_{1\perp} + p_{2\perp} = 0$, so the two nuclei must gain equal and opposite transverse momentum.
That means the two outgoing paths must lie on opposite sides of the incoming line, one with an upward component and one with a downward component.
Diagrams A, B and D all show one track deflected to one side and the other track to the other side, so cancellation of transverse momentum is possible.
Only the diagram with both outgoing tracks on the same side below the incoming line gives two transverse momenta in the same direction, which cannot sum to zero. This is option C.

options.A: The two paths leave on opposite sides of the incoming line, so upward momentum of one can cancel downward momentum of the other.
options.B: One path is deflected upward and the other slightly downward, so total momentum perpendicular to the incoming direction can still be zero.
options.C: Both paths after collision lie on the same side of the incoming line, giving a net momentum perpendicular to the initial direction which cannot be conserved.
options.D: The paths leave on opposite sides of the incoming line, so the perpendicular components can cancel while the forward components add to the initial momentum.
